statement: This session is entirely about distributed ID generators.
detail: The teacher opens with "The third day second" - possibly meaning week 3, day 2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's all about distributed ID generators.
flags: check: "The third day second" as heard - third week, second day?

statement: Distributed ID generation is one of the most misunderstood topics: people think auto-increment solves it and that it is no big problem.
detail: Part of the phrase is garbled ("auto increment [unclear: works giving ID wise this] such a big problem").
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like this is one of the most misunderstood topic out there.

statement: Most people do not face the ID generation problem until they hit scale, but because of mass internet penetration most companies now hit that scale sooner than they think - which is where distributed ID generators come in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: most companies hit that scale sooner than they think.

statement: A second reason to learn ID generators in depth is the beauty of the computer science behind them: the solutions engineers devised are going to blow your mind.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there's some beauty of computer science going behind the scenes.
flags: check: "in the device solutions" as heard - devising solutions?

statement: A third reason: understanding ID generation reveals some really interesting side effects that most people never think about.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when we understand ID generation, we see some really interesting side effects of that, which most people didn't even think about.

statement: Lecture plan: first a journey through the basics of ID generation to build foundational ideas, then how Amazon, Flickr, Twitter and Instagram do it, plus a demo-like look at an interesting side effect.
detail: In the break announcement (part 2) the side effect is named as pagination.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How Amazon does it. How Flickr does it. How Twitter does it. How Instagram does it.

statement: Implement every one of the ID generation approaches yourself: theory is fine, but past-cohort participants who implemented them got a much deeper understanding of why each one works.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: implement every single one of these to get the deep understanding, why that works

statement: An ID gives uniqueness to a particular row, document, object or event: anything that helps you uniquely identify something is its ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is more about giving uniqueness to a particular row, document, object, event, whatnot.

statement: Problem statement: assign a globally unique ID to anything that asks for one - i.e. write a function that spits out something unique every time it is invoked.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we write a function that spits out something unique every time it is invoked.

statement: Do not jump directly to a central ID service: start with an ID generation function that is part of your business/application logic, invoked locally per request; the evolution to a central ID service comes later.
detail: The teacher says many people start writing a new service for ID generation immediately; he constrains the problem to a local function to build the foundation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the function we are writing is not a central service. Don't directly jump into that.

statement: Simplest starting point: since time is unique and always moves forward, the ID function can just return the current epoch millisecond.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: why can't our ID generation function just return my current epoch millisecond?

statement: Returning epoch milliseconds should work but something must break - otherwise everyone would be using it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if it was the case, then everyone would be using this.

statement: Using epoch milliseconds means accepting millisecond granularity: the function cannot be invoked twice within the same millisecond, otherwise you have to go to microsecond or nanosecond level.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this function cannot be invoked twice within the same millisecond. Otherwise you have to go to microsecond and nanosecond level.

statement: With multiple machines, the same epoch-millisecond function can run on two machines within the same millisecond; both return the same value (e.g. 1729), so IDs collide and are not globally unique.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Both would generate the same ID because what we were just returning was 1729, the current epoch millisecond

statement: To resolve the multi-machine collision, concatenate machine ID and epoch millisecond, giving IDs like M1-1729 and M2-1729 that are globally unique.
detail: M1/M2 is just the teacher's nomenclature; you can change it however you want.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: concatenate machine ID and epoch millisecond.

statement: Standard collision-resolution practice: whenever you see a collision, add to the ID the thing that led to that collision (here, the machine ID).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever you see a collision, you try to add something that led to that collision in order to resolve the collision.

statement: If the program has threads, the same function can run multiple times within the same millisecond on the same machine (threads on multiple cores), so machine ID + epoch ms can again collide (two threads both producing M1-1729).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: two threads executing at the same time within the same machine would spit out that exact same ID M1-1729.

statement: Thread IDs are typically integers assigned by the operating system (T1, T2 are just a simplification).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These are typically integer thread IDs, which operating system assigns to the thread.

statement: First approach for threads: concatenate machine ID, thread ID and epoch millisecond, giving IDs like M1-T1-1729 and M1-T2-1729.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Concatenate machine ID, thread ID and get epoch milliseconds.

statement: Second approach for threads: instead of a thread ID, add a counter (a common practice is one that resets every few minutes).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Other way to do it is by adding a counter that resets every few minutes. It's a very common practice.

statement: Always appending the thing that led to the conflict leads to gigantic IDs; a static counter avoids that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you always adding the thing that led to conflict leads to gigantic, that which leads to basically gigantic IDs.

statement: A static counter is a globally allocated variable on the heap that every thread can access; atomically incrementing it each time the function is invoked resolves thread collisions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: static counter is globally allocated variable on heap. Everyone can access that.

statement: ID logic with counter: getid concatenates machine ID, timestamp and a static counter that is incremented (counter++) on every call, e.g. M1-1729-01, M1-1729-02, M1-1729-03, then M1-1730-...; with an atomic increment there is never a collision within the same machine no matter how many threads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: getid function in all is concatenation of machine ID, timestamp and a static counter.

statement: The counter increment must be atomic (thread-safe): it is not atomic by default, so wrap it in locks/mutexes or use a native atomic library.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's not by default atomic, you wrap it in locks and whatnot, or do an atom or use a native atomic library to do that.

statement: When to reset the counter (every few minutes or seconds) is business logic; IDs stay unique because the millisecond part moves forward anyway, as long as the counter does not exceed the integer limit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every few minutes you can reset the counter or every few seconds you can reset the counter. That's your business logic.

statement: Two ways to resolve collisions between threads: append the thread ID, or use an atomically incremented static counter that works no matter how many threads there are.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One is by appending thread ID and second is by using a static count.

statement: Given an atomically increasing counter, the time component is redundant: the counter alone always gives 1, 2, 3, ..., so time can be removed and IDs become shorter - ID = machine ID + counter (m101, m102, m103).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: given that the counter is atomically increasing, time is redundant.

statement: Limitation of machine ID + counter: the counter can hit the integer limit (about 4 billion); with 2^64 it is a massive number you might never hit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when it hits the integer limit, that's a 4 billion, or if it's 2 raised to 64, that's a massive number.

statement: Machine ID concatenated with an atomically incremented static counter solves the uniqueness problem (summary of the common ways seen so far).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Machine ID concatenated with a static counter, which is atomically increment. This solves the problem.

statement: Problem with a static counter: it lives in volatile memory with no persistence, so when the process or machine reboots the counter resets to zero and the machine regenerates IDs (m101, m102, ...) it already issued - the logic is no longer unique.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As soon as your machine reboots, what would happen? This counter would again be reset to zero

statement: The root cause of the reboot problem is that the counter is stored in volatile memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The root cause of this problem is that the place at which we are storing the counter is actually a volatile memory.

statement: A student proposes backing the counter up with a file locally; the teacher accepts it because volatility is the problem.
detail: Teacher: "You write it to the file locally, right? Because volatility is the problem."
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Back it up with the file locally.

statement: File-backed counter logic: counter = load() from disk when the process starts; on every getid do counter++, immediately save the counter to disk (e.g. open a text file and dump it), then concatenate machine ID and counter.
detail: The business logic remains the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever a function is invoked, I do count++ and immediately save the counter to the disk.

statement: Loading the counter from disk once at process start/boot is fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One time at startup of my process or boot up of a machine, it's fine.

statement: Saving the counter on every ID generation causes a disk IO per invocation: at a high invocation rate this puts a lot of pressure on the disk with many micro disk IOs (problem 1).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every time that my ID function is getting invoked, I am doing a disk IO.

statement: Problem 2 of a disk write per ID: it affects latency, because you do disk IO every time instead of serving the ID from memory.
detail: Literally "reduce the latency"; the contrast drawn is disk IO every time vs serving from memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Problem number two is it might reduce the latency that you are looking at

statement: A student proposes adding a third part to the ID: a boot counter read from the file at server startup, incremented and written back once; each server startup gets a new value, and the static counter starts from zero in memory without being saved on every call.
detail: The teacher first questions how it solves frequent disk IO, then understands and accepts: "Okay, okay. That's a good one." Nothing is stored per call.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So each server startup is represented by a new counter.

statement: Downside of the boot-counter approach: the increment at server startup must be atomic (it can be made atomic), and the ID gets longer.
detail: Answered by the student when the teacher asked for the downside; "That's right" and "Correct. Longer ID." appear inside the student's turn (may be the teacher confirming).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: When you increment at server startup, that will have to be atomic. That's right. That can be made atomic. A longer ID
flags: check: speaker of "That's right" / "Correct. Longer ID." inside the student's turn

statement: The teacher praises the boot-counter approach as really good because it tackles the disk IO problem head on, says the long ID might become a (not big) problem whose disadvantages will be discussed, and says he will add this approach to the course going forward.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your approach is really good. That approach is really good. But that long ID might become a problem.

statement: A student proposes a bank of IDs: on reading the counter (e.g. 1), add 1000 and store it; IDs are then served from memory, and on reaching 2000 you read and add 1000 again - 1000 iterations in memory per write.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: maybe we can have some bank of IDs. For example, first time I read it is one, just add 1000 to it and store it.

statement: The teacher reframes the bank-of-IDs proposal as writing to disk periodically at a certain frequency instead of every time, slashing the number of disk IOs; he stresses this approach because it comes in handy at two different places.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are minimizing the number of times you have to write to the disk by writing in a periodic manner.

statement: Flush frequency: instead of saving the counter every time, write it to disk only every N IDs (e.g. every 1000), cutting disk IO by a factor of 1000 - a massive performance gain.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: after generating every thousand IDs, I'll write it to the disk.

statement: Flushing every 1000 IDs cuts disk IO by a factor of 1000.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are literally slashing on disk IO by a factor of 1000, which is a massive performance.

statement: Flush-frequency logic: at startup, counter = load() + flush frequency (to avoid collisions); on each call do counter++ and if counter mod 1000 == 0, write the counter to disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So our logic now becomes counter equal to load plus the flush frequency.
flags: check: "collision at up" - words may be missing

statement: Worked example with flush frequency 3: machine M1 generates 1, 2, 3 (3 mod 3 = 0, so 3 is flushed), then 4, 5, 6 (6 flushed), then 7, 8 and the machine crashes. The last value on disk is 6 but 8 was already issued; restarting from 6 would regenerate 7 and 8, which is wrong.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When the machine crashed, the last value that was written was 6. The ID that was generated was already 8.

statement: On recovery, start from the safest value: the last flushed value plus the flush frequency plus one (in the example, 9 + 1 = 10, giving M1-10, M1-11, M1-12, with the next flush at 12).
detail: As spoken: "nine plus one, 10" (6 + 3 = 9, then + 1); the earlier code said counter = load + flush frequency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The last value that was flushed plus the flush frequency plus one. So nine plus one, 10.

statement: Starting from the safest value leaks some integers (8 and 9 are never used), which is fine: correctness of the system matters more than utilizing every single integer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Given that the correctness of the system matters more than you left you utilizing every single integer out there, right?

statement: Key takeaway 1: do not do IO every time - add a periodicity factor, implemented as simply as a mod operation (n mod N, then write), not a thread with a timer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now don't think of a thread and timer and I'll do it. Think of very simple approach, as simple as a mod operation.

statement: Key takeaway 2: whenever a machine recovers, start from the safest value; always think of correctness. These are key design constraints when designing a distributed ID generator.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever your machine recovers, quote unquote, you start from the safest value.

statement: The IDs generated so far (machine ID + counter) have no particular order: with hundreds of thousands of machines, M1 can be literally anything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: these IDs have no particular order, like M1 can be literally anything.

statement: New constraint: globally monotonically increasing IDs - no matter how many machines generate IDs or where a request goes, each later request gets a larger ID (e.g. 1, 2, 5, 6 across 10 machines).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if I want to enforce a monotonically increasing constraint to my IDs?

statement: Why monotonicity matters: in the week-2 airline check-in system, transactions T1 and T2 were ordered by their numbers - 1 and 2 tell which transaction came first.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How did we know the transaction T1 came before transaction T2?

statement: Ordered IDs help conflict resolution: with a strategy where the newer write overrides the older write, the larger number (2) identifies the newer write, so you accept the write made by the newer transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one of the conflict strategy would be the newer write overrides the older write.

statement: Monotonically increasing IDs play a very important role in conflict resolution - one of the places, not all the places, where they are needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: monotonically increasing IDs play a very important role in doing conflict resolution

statement: Monotonically increasing does not mean purely sequential: 1 2 3 4 5 6 is strictly sequential, but 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 is also monotonically increasing - each new ID is guaranteed greater than all previous IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: my next ID that is generated is guaranteed to be greater than all the previous IDs that are generated.

statement: Flip the order to time then machine ID: since time always moves forward and occupies the most significant bits, IDs get a natural order (e.g. 17290001, 17290002) - pretty decent but not strict monotonicity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if we flip the order and have concatenation of time and then machine ID?

statement: In a time-first ID, the time part forms the most significant bits; the lower part can be the machine ID or, perfectly fine, a counter.
detail: "You can also change this to counters, perfectly fine."
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These are the most significant bits of my number.

statement: Within the same millisecond time-first IDs can be misordered: the first request may go to machine 2 and the next to machine 1, giving 17290002 then 17290001; once the millisecond passes, IDs are almost monotonically increasing across the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So in that case, what you get is 17290002 first and then 17290001.

statement: Time-first IDs stay stateless (a request can go to any machine) and give almost-monotonic IDs with excellent throughput at minimal cost, without maintaining central state; some incorrectness is accepted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: without having to maintain a central state of things in order to get those things increasing

statement: Assuming the machine ID is an integer, the time-first ID is just bits: time concatenated with machine ID as one number.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Assume machine ID is integer and then it's just bits.

statement: This is why you see time on the leftmost side of ID generators - pick any: as time moves forward the number is always greater, giving natural ordering.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would always see time sitting on the leftmost side. This is the reason why.

statement: Time-first IDs are a good solution but still do not guarantee monotonicity; within-millisecond misordering (machine 2 then machine 1) is one reason.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: although it's a good solution, but it still does not guarantee monotonicity.

statement: A second problem is on the time side: the design assumed all machines' clocks are perfectly synchronized, which is not the case - clocks go out of sync.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we assume that the time across all of my machines is exactly synchronous, but basically perfectly synchronized, which is not the case.

statement: It is very common for servers to go out of sync, so SRE/DevOps teams run a process (job) that periodically syncs machine clocks to NTP servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have a process that is running, which is continuously syncing NTP clocks of your servers.

statement: Clocks go out of sync because the machine clock is a hardware clock: a quartz crystal vibrating at a particular frequency in your laptop/server/CPU, whose vibrations are measured to tell that a second or millisecond has passed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is a quartz crystal vibrating in your machine, in your laptop, on your server, in your CPU.

statement: Physics analogy: giving energy to a thing makes it vibrate faster - water heated by fire boils; taking energy out makes it freeze into ice; this holds for every element.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you throw energy at a thing, it vibrates faster.

statement: Heat (e.g. a high-intensity game heating the CPU) makes the quartz crystal vibrate faster so the clock runs fast; an extremely cold environment slows the vibration so the clock runs slow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Quartz crystal would start to vibrate faster and your clock would move faster.

statement: Because physical phenomena speed up or slow down the computer clock, a periodic job is needed to keep clocks in sync, and it runs more frequently than you think.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is why there is a need of a periodic job that keeps the clock in sync, and it runs more frequently than you think.

statement: Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat of Google once chased a bug caused by a bit flipped by a natural phenomenon (an explosion or a solar storm); the teacher recommends the article "the friendship that made Google special" - you cannot run away from nature.
detail: The teacher loves the papers Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat wrote.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just Google "friendship that made Google special".

statement: Even assuming clocks are periodically and eventually synced with NTP, until then a clock may be out of sync at the moment an ID is generated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: up until then, there is a chance that your clock is out of sync when your ID is getting generated.

statement: Clock-skew example: machines 2, 4, 7, 9 have times 23, 24, 23, 23; requests in order to M2, M4, M7, M9 produce time+machine IDs 232, 244, 237, 239 - not monotonically increasing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the ID that would be generated on M2 would be 232, then the next ID would be generated would be 244, then 237
flags: asr: [?epoch milliseconds | asr: "a pop many seconds"]

statement: Where monotonicity is needed, clock skew must be taken care of because it affects the correctness of the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even the clock skewness is what you need to take care of.

statement: Ensuring strict monotonicity across a distributed system where ID generation logic is distributed is almost impossible - the teacher did not find a theoretical proof, but practically too many things can break it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ensuring monotonicity across distributed systems is almost impossible.

statement: Central ID generation service: one machine; whoever wants an ID makes a network call to the ID server, which generates an ID and sends it back (throughput concerns deferred).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whoever wants the ID makes a network call, ID server generates an ID and sends it back.

statement: On a single machine, clock skew does not break ordering: when NTP sync finds the clock is ahead (24 instead of 23), the clock does not jump back; it slows its counting until real time catches up, so the clock never goes back in time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Your clock slows down the counting and then it catches up and then it starts from 24.
flags: check: "and then it receives" - unclear ending

statement: Always remember: the clock never goes back in time on a single machine - it can slow down or speed up, but always moves forward.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So always remember, the clock never goes back in time. Never.

statement: If ID generation sticks to one server, its clock always moves forward, so it always produces monotonically increasing IDs regardless of where requests come from.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the clock on this machine is always moving forward, it will always have monotonically increasing IDs.

statement: A single central ID server is a single point of failure, so for fault tolerance you add one more machine behind a load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But having this one machine is a single point of failure.

statement: With two ID servers, whichever gets a request must talk to the other ID server to see the last ID it generated, increase it plus some buffer, and only then generate a new ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it needs to connect, to talk to other ID server to see what was the last ID that it generated.

statement: Two ID servers would need to constantly gossip about generated IDs to agree each new one is larger than any ever generated; this makes simple ID generation super complex and loses throughput - high-throughput continuous gossip becomes very messy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: these two servers need to constantly gossip about the IDs that they generated

statement: You cannot have an ID generation service that is distributed in nature and also guarantees strict monotonicity at high throughput - not possible.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you cannot have an ID generation service which is distributed in nature, which also guarantees strict monotonicity at high throughput.

statement: Every fix brings a new problem or constraint, so people relax constraints, because not everyone needs monotonicity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because not everyone needs monotonicity.

statement: Objection: "but MySQL server has monotonic IDs". Answer: MySQL is a single machine, not distributed; the ID logic is part of the database engine, which is why you see IDs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The ID logic is part of your database engine. It's a single machine.

statement: If MySQL were distributed (multi-master), you would never get monotonic auto-increment IDs: put MySQL in multi-master mode with an auto-increment ID and see the number of conflicts, because each master is its own brain.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Try putting MySQL server in multi-master mode with an auto-increment ID. See the number of conflicts you get

statement: Everything in computer science and software engineering is a trade-off: you get something, you lose something - always.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: everything in software engineering is a trade-off. You have to lose something.

statement: When you need ID generation (or similar), ask whether you really need the constraints you were given: challenge them with critical questions - is it OK if IDs are not integers, are random like UUIDs/GUIDs, or are not monotonic?
detail: In most cases requirements say monotonicity is needed, but after a couple of critical questions it may turn out otherwise, because not everyone thinks it through.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: always see that, do you really need these constraints?

statement: Why we need ID generation at all even though MySQL/MongoDB give IDs: with a sharded / multi-master database (e.g. two MySQL servers both in master mode, writes going anywhere), the servers don't talk to each other, so each auto-increments 1, 2, 3, 4 independently and IDs collide.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: these two servers do not communicate or do not talk to each other, correct?

statement: With multi-master databases you cannot rely on database IDs; you need your own custom ID logic (e.g. concatenating machine ID) to uniquely identify entries - which is where distributed ID generators are needed; the four company examples will show practical use.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you have your databases operating in multi-master mode, you would typically see a custom ID generation logic in place

statement: A student asks whether, instead of a shared ID service, a common database with locks would work; the teacher answers it would be unique, but that database is itself a shared service on a single machine - one and the same thing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, it will be unique, but that is still a single machine, right? That is, that database itself becomes a service, right?

statement: A student asks how to resolve conflicts based on IDs when IDs in a distributed system may not be unique/ordered; the teacher defers it - only about 30 percent of the topic is done.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: we are still only basically 30 percent done, and we'll talk about that

statement: A student proposes that multi-master servers auto-increment by the number of servers (with two: one gives 0, 2, 4 and the other 1, 3, 5); the teacher says it can be done but has a slight disadvantage to be discussed later.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: can't be like auto increment by like the number of servers we have, basically?
flags: unclear: "i have it covered f5 right"

statement: A student asks why not append a random ID instead of a static counter; the teacher: the static counter was chosen for monotonicity, which a random ID does not give - if you can relax that constraint, use a random ID like a UUID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Random ID does not give you monotonicity.

statement: You may think you need monotonicity, but in reality you can often relax that constraint - and then a random ID like a UUID works.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You may think you need monotonicity, but in reality, you can relax those constraints

statement: Why not use a UUID instead of all this complexity? You can, if it is okay to relax the constraint - not everyone needs strict monotonicity; but with UUIDs you lose ordering (you get some, you lose some).
detail: The ordering point was voiced by a student ("we will not be able to... give that ordering") and the teacher replied "You get some, you lose some."
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relax the constraint. If it's okay for you to relax the constraint, then use UUID.
flags: check: speaker - "Got it. Got it." may be Student 3

statement: UUIDs, MongoDB IDs and similar will be covered later: where to use them, their disadvantages, and how monotonicity helps in real practical situations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll talk about MongoDB IDs, UUIDs and whatnot.

statement: A student proposes a distributed set of ID servers, each appending its own server ID to the IDs it generates; the teacher says the approach is also correct but loses monotonicity, which is fine.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: they just append their own ID server to that logic which is generating IDs.
flags: check: speaker - may be Student 2 continuing after "just a second"

statement: There is no one right way to do ID generation: each approach gains in some places and loses in others; it is a trade-off between what you want and what you can give up while maximizing throughput, performance and efficiency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is no one right way to do it.

statement: So far the lecture covers only the core idea behind ID generation; the specific company examples will show what each design gains and loses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm just discussing on the core idea behind ID generation.

statement: A student proposes avoiding periodic saves: on restart, read the last counter/message ID saved in the database (max row ID) and increment from there.
detail: Teacher: that is exactly what the load function does; the proposal assumes every generated ID is written back to the database as a row, which is an expensive call - the ID logic here does not assume that. A challenge at 00:52:35 is labelled Student? but sounds like the teacher.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: when the server restarts, we read from the database, get the last counter saved in the database, and then start incrementing ahead?

statement: Restarting from the max row ID saved in the database is exactly what the load function already does (load from disk or database - one and the same thing): you start from that particular point.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's exactly what this load is actually doing.

statement: The max-row-ID proposal assumes an entry is inserted in the database for every generated ID and then the max row is picked; the teacher's ID logic deliberately does not assume that, because writing back to the database is expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are assuming that an entry is getting created in the database for every single thing.

statement: The ID generation logic should not assume each generated ID is written back to a database (that is expensive); the ID may just be attached to something and pushed forward, like a request ID.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You're just attaching something in this, basically pushing it forward. Let's say request ID kind of thing.
